healthcareSystem: State-funded system for residents. Tourists pay out-of-pocket. Private clinics in Baku offer decent care.
qualityNotes: Private clinics in Baku provide reasonable care with some English-speaking staff. Public hospitals are underfunded and quality is inconsistent. Healthcare outside Baku is very limited.
pharmacyHours: Most pharmacies open 8am-8pm; some 24/7 pharmacies in Baku
pharmacyTips: Look for 'Aptek' signs. Pharmacies are common in Baku. Many medications available without prescription. Pharmacists typically speak Azerbaijani and Russian; English is rare.
prescriptionRules: Many medications available OTC with relaxed enforcement. Antibiotics are widely sold without prescription. Foreign prescriptions are generally not accepted. Visit a local clinic for a local prescription if needed for controlled substances.

restrictedMeds.name: Controlled narcotics (opioids, tramadol)
restrictedMeds.note: Strictly controlled. Carry a doctor's letter and original prescription.

restrictedMeds.name: Psychotropic medications (stimulants, benzodiazepines)
restrictedMeds.note: Some psychiatric medications are controlled. Bring documentation.

restrictedMeds.name: Cannabis-based products
restrictedMeds.note: Cannabis is illegal in all forms in Azerbaijan, including CBD products.

bringDocumentation: Carry a doctor's letter in English listing all medications with generic names. Keep medications in original packaging. For controlled substances, bring the original prescription. A Russian or Azerbaijani translation is helpful but not required.

travelInsurance.tips: Travel insurance is strongly recommended. Private clinics in Baku are affordable but costs add up. Medical evacuation coverage is important if visiting rural or mountainous areas. Some policies exclude conflict zones near Nagorno-Karabakh.

vaccinations.notes: No mandatory vaccinations for entry. Ensure routine vaccinations are up to date.

waterNotes: Tap water in Baku is treated but bottled water is recommended. In rural areas, always drink bottled or boiled water. Water quality outside Baku is unreliable.
foodSafetyTips: Food in established restaurants is generally safe. Azerbaijani cuisine is well-cooked (kebabs, plov, dolma). Be cautious with salads and raw vegetables at roadside eateries. Wash fruits before eating.
medicalTourismNote: Azerbaijan is developing medical tourism, particularly dental care and wellness/spa treatments. Baku has new private hospital facilities aiming to attract international patients.
metaDescription: Complete health & medication guide for traveling to Azerbaijan. Emergency 112, pharmacy tips, hospital info, vaccination advice, and insurance guidance.

hospitals.notes: Private clinic with modern facilities. Some English-speaking staff.

hospitals.name: Central Neftchilar Hospital
hospitals.notes: Public hospital with emergency department. Azerbaijani and Russian speaking. Bring a translator.

hospitals.name: International SOS Baku Clinic
hospitals.notes: International clinic focused on expat and traveler healthcare. Direct insurance billing.

dentalCare.availability: Dental care available in Baku at private clinics. Good quality for basic procedures.
dentalCare.costRange: $15-40 for a consultation; $20-70 for fillings; $15-50 for extractions
dentalCare.notes: Private dental clinics in Baku offer modern equipment at affordable prices. Quality outside Baku is limited.
dentalCare.emergencyTip: For dental emergencies in Baku, visit a private dental clinic (diş klinikası). Several clinics near the Old City accept walk-in emergency patients.

mentalHealth.internationalLine: No dedicated English-language crisis line — contact your embassy
mentalHealth.englishTherapists: Very limited. Some available through international clinics in Baku. Sessions typically $30-50.
mentalHealth.notes: Mental health services in English are very scarce. International clinics in Baku are the best option. Stigma around mental health is significant.

accessibilityInfo.overview: Accessibility infrastructure is limited. Baku's newer developments have some accessibility features, but the Old City and older areas are challenging.
accessibilityInfo.hospitalAccess: Private hospitals in Baku are generally wheelchair accessible. Older facilities may lack proper access.
accessibilityInfo.transport: Baku Metro has limited accessibility. Newer buses have low-floor access. Taxis are the most practical option.
accessibilityInfo.tips: Baku's Old City (Icherisheher) has cobblestone streets and steep inclines challenging for wheelchairs. Newer parts of Baku are more accessible.

covidStatus.entryRequirements: No COVID testing or vaccination requirements for entry as of 2026.
covidStatus.maskPolicy: No mask mandates. Masks are uncommon.
covidStatus.testing: Tests available at private clinics and labs in Baku. Rapid tests: 15-25 AZN ($9-15); PCR: 30-50 AZN ($18-30).
covidStatus.notes: All COVID entry restrictions have been lifted.

insuranceClaimProcess: Private clinics in Baku may accept direct billing from international insurers (particularly SOS International partners). Otherwise, pay upfront and keep all receipts and documentation. Request English-language documents. File claims upon return.

commonCosts.note: Estimated typical out-of-pocket costs at private facilities. Healthcare is affordable by Western standards.

medicalEvacuation.note: Istanbul is the primary evacuation destination due to flight connectivity and hospital quality. For less urgent cases, Baku's private hospitals can handle most conditions.
